For positive score p and K uniform-negative scores n_j, uncorrected candidate CE is log(1+Σ_j exp(n_j−p)); sampled BCE is softplus(−p)+Σ_j softplus(n_j), before reduction. At K=1, candidate CE equals softplus(n−p), exactly BPR logistic loss; BCE remains different. CE compares relative scores and is invariant to a shared score shift; BCE anchors absolute logits. [Theoretical analysis](https://arxiv.org/html/2411.07770v2) confirms the K=1 equivalence and cautions against assuming full-catalog CE advantages transfer to sampled objectives.

Direct algebra: CE gradients are q_positive−1 and q_negative, coupling candidates through softmax; BCE gradients are σ(p)−1 and σ(n_j), independently. Summing versus averaging all K+1 BCE terms changes gradient scale; averaging negatives separately also changes positive/negative weighting. A negative repeated m times contributes m·exp(n) to CE’s denominator—equivalent to an effective n+log(m)—and m copies of its BCE term. Keep replacement/deduplication identical. Uncorrected candidate CE is not an unbiased full-catalog softmax estimator merely because negatives are uniform.

[gSASRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.07192) attributes sampled-BCE problems to overconfidence and reports improvements from more negatives plus gBCE; these findings do not establish candidate-CE superiority for this BERT4Rec task. [Gold Loss](https://github.com/antklen/sasrec-bert4rec-recsys23) likewise identifies loss and negative count as major comparison confounders. Minimal control: if the proposal changes BCE/K=1 to CE/K=M, add BCE/K=M using identical sampled candidates, masking, architecture, updates and documented reduction. This separates the negative-count effect under BCE from the loss effect at M. A full 2×2 adds CE/K=1. Each trial retains one independently trained BERT4Rec checkpoint per category; select using fixed macro validation HR@10.
